sentences.text: One buyer said "we pay for what we bill, so it has to follow our usage", and a controller wanted revenue recognized "the day usage posts".
On the objection side, one buyer was "worried about invoice surprises for our customers".
The most common signer in this segment is the Finance leader.
Across 212 opportunities, the segment shows a 38% win rate, a $41k median deal size and a 78 days won-deal cycle.
One buyer wanted an "audit trail for every charge" and said "regulators ask for it".
One CFO objected that "the finance team is only two people".
One buyer also looked at a competing vendor; separately, the segment shows 96 opportunities, a 29% win rate, a $36k median deal size and a won-deal cycle of 64 days.
In Developer tools, one buyer said "engineers want an api first billing layer".
One buyer objected that "we can build this ourselves in a quarter", and another said the "security review took longer than the eval".
The most common signer is the Head of engineering, across 143 opportunities with a 22% win rate and a median deal size of $29k.
In healthcare software, one [security lead] needed HIPAA terms before any call.
Another buyer said legal wanted a BAA and "we could not give one".
A third buyer raised the length of their "procurement process".
Separately, the segment shows a 9% win rate across 77 opportunities, a $52k median deal size and a won-deal cycle of 131 days.
Across 58 opportunities, marketplaces show a 17% win rate and a $33k median deal size, and one buyer objected that "our payouts are the hard part, not invoices".
A VP finance said that take rate revenue is not billing.
Another buyer objected that "this does not touch our seller fees".
DACH shows a 12% win rate across 44 opportunities, and won deals took 102 days.
One buyer objected that a German entity "needs local invoicing rules", and a controller said they "only works with local vendors".
The most common signer is not found in the data, and one buyer said "org charts are private here".
One buyer said they "already live in Salesforce and want quotes to flow to billing".
Another buyer said a competitor "came up because of the Salesforce connector".
Across 310 opportunities in this segment, the win rate is 27% and the median deal size is $44k.
On why companies buy, one buyer in the CFO role wants "one system for all business units".
On objections, one buyer said "we need a six month legal review", and another said "five stakeholders have to approve".

sentences.text: Brazil has 9 opportunities at a 56% win rate.
One buyer gave a reason to buy: "marketplaces here bill in reais and need local tax".
In the seat pricing segment, the win rate is 14% across 180 opportunities.
One buyer objected that "seat based is a poor fit for usage billing" and kept their existing tool.
One buyer said metering by gigabyte was the hard part, and another said "we bill per terabyte and need it exact".
On the objection side, one [controller] doubts revenue recognition for prepaid commits.
In logistics software, one buyer in the [VP ops] role wants "invoices to follow shipments".
One buyer objected that "per shipment pricing makes forecasting hard".
Another buyer said a competing billing vendor was "the incumbent".
Separately, the segment shows 64 opportunities, a 19% win rate and a median deal size of $31k, and no signer data is available.
In Education, the win rate is 11% across 39 opportunities.
One buyer chose the product for "term based billing".
One buyer objected that "budgets are set once a year".
The most common signer is the Finance leader.
In Media, one controller liked that "ad impressions can be billed directly".
One buyer objected that "ad credits are messy to recognize".
One buyer asked about a competing product.
Separately, the segment shows a 21% win rate across 47 opportunities, and won deals took 59 days; no figure shows who signs.
In E-commerce, with 102 opportunities, a 16% win rate and a median deal size of $24k, one buyer gave as a reason to buy that "subscription boxes need proration done right".
One buyer objected that they already use a billing add on.
A CFO objected that "checkout is handled by the shop platform".
Government shows a 6% win rate across 31 opportunities, and won deals took 190 days to close.
One buyer reported that an elected official wants "a public tender first".
A controller said they "cannot sign without a framework contract".
One fintech buyer said usage based fees "map to how our banks bill us".
A controller at one buyer said they compared the product with a competitor.
Separately, the segment shows a 25% win rate across 301 opportunities, with a median deal size of $39k.
One IT services buyer said "resellers need billing that sums usage across clients" as a reason to buy.
Separately, the segment shows a 13% win rate across 66 opportunities.
One buyer in the mixed pricing segment sells seats plus overage and said they "need both on one invoice", while a [VP finance] buyer wants "one source of revenue truth".
One buyer noted that a competitor "handled seats but not overage".
One objection raised was "migration risk during quarter close".
The most common signer is the Finance leader, and the segment shows a 24% win rate across 155 opportunities, with a median deal size of $37k and a won-deal cycle of 83 days.
One buyer said they "expect usage billing to matter once we launch tiers", which points to a future need rather than a current one.
Another buyer pushed back that "a spreadsheet works for us for now".
A third buyer raised price, saying they want "a cheap tool".
Separately, this segment shows a 10% win rate across 240 opportunities, with a median deal size of $12k.
Add a rule to the ideal customer profile that the pricing model equals Usage.
Across 212 opportunities with usage pricing, deals won at 38% (range 32% to 45%), clearly higher than the 16% win rate for the rest.
Add a rule to the ideal customer profile that gives a weight of 15 to accounts whose pricing model equals Usage.
Across 212 opportunities with usage pricing, deals won at 38% (range 32% to 45%) against 16% for the rest, a clearly higher result, while 190 seat-priced opportunities won at 16%.
Add a rule to the ideal customer profile that gives weight 10 to accounts whose Industry equals Fintech.
Across 140 Fintech opportunities the deals showed a 32% win rate (range 25% to 40%), compared with 18% for the rest, which is clearly higher.
Add a rule that gives weight to accounts where the Signer role findable trait is Yes.
Across 300 opportunities where the signer role was findable (Yes), deals won at 29% (range 24% to 34%), compared with 14% for the rest, a clearly higher result.

sentences.text: Add a rule that gives weight 5 to accounts whose Technology includes NetSuite.
Across 95 opportunities, deals with NetSuite won 32% of the time (range 23% to 41%) compared with 19% for the rest, a clearly higher win rate, and the most common loss reason was timing.
Add a rule to the ideal customer profile that scores accounts in the 120 to 499 size band, with a weight of 12.
Across 400 opportunities, deals in the 120 to 499 size band won 30% of the time (range 26% to 35%) against 15% for the rest, which is clearly higher.
Remove the rule that favors accounts whose Technology includes Salesforce from the ideal customer profile.

Across 310 opportunities, Salesforce accounts won 27% of deals (range 22% to 32%) against 22% for the rest, but the deals showed this gap is explained by company size rather than the technology itself.
Remove the rule that favors accounts whose Technology includes HubSpot.
Across 180 opportunities, HubSpot accounts won 24% of the time (range 19% to 31%) against 23% for the rest, and the deals showed that gap is explained by size rather than by HubSpot.
Remove the rule that targets accounts with an HQ city of Austin from the ideal customer profile.
Across 70 opportunities, Austin deals won at 17% (range 10% to 28%) against 16% for the rest, so the deals showed no clear difference.
We are removing the rule that favors companies with a founding year after 2015.
Across 260 opportunities, companies founded after 2015 won 21% of deals, with a range of 17% to 27%, against 20% for the rest, and the deals showed this gap is explained by company size.
We will give accounts on usage pricing more weight in the ideal customer profile, with a weight of 20.
Across 212 opportunities, deals with usage pricing won 38% of the time (range 32% to 45%), compared with 16% for all other deals, a clearly higher win rate.
Give accounts in the 120 to 1,999 size band more weight in the ideal customer profile, with a weight of 6.
Across 520 opportunities in this size band, deals won 29% of the time (range 25% to 33%), clearly higher than the 14% win rate for all other deals.
The Industry weight for Developer tools changes to 4 in the ideal customer profile.
Across 143 opportunities, Developer tools deals won at 22% (range 16% to 30%), the same as the 22% for all other deals, so the result is not clear.
Add Healthcare software as an excluded industry in the ideal customer profile.
Across 77 opportunities, Healthcare software deals won 9% of the time (range 4% to 18%) against 23% for the rest, a clearly lower win rate, with compliance as the top loss reason.
Add Government to the Industry exclusions in the ideal customer profile.
Across 31 Government opportunities the win rate was 6% (range 2% to 21%), clearly lower than 21% for the rest, and the top loss reason was timing.
Add Brazil as an excluded country in the ideal customer profile.
Across 9 opportunities, deals in Brazil won 56% of the time against 17% for other countries, but the range of 27% to 81% leaves the result not clear.
Accounts in the 2,000 to 4,999 size band will now score lower in the ideal customer profile.
Across 121 opportunities in this band the win rate was 8% (range 5% to 15%), clearly lower than 17% for the rest, and the most common loss reason was no decision.
Healthcare software accounts will now carry a penalty in the Industry score, so they rank lower in the ideal customer profile.
Across 77 Healthcare software opportunities the win rate was 9% (range 4% to 18%), against 23% for the rest, and compliance was the most common loss reason.
Deals in the DACH region will now count against fit in the ideal customer profile.
Across 44 opportunities, DACH deals won 11% of the time (range 5% to 24%), compared with 20% for all other regions, which is clearly lower.
Add a rule to the profile that gives credit to accounts whose Country is United States.
Across 650 opportunities in the United States the deals won 23% of the time (range 20% to 26%) against 24% for the rest, so the evidence is not clear.
